topic: Notes on a sum of products of Epstein-type zeta functions Z(s,ω)Z(1−s,ω) and its relation to Kronecker's limit formula, followed by arguments that the common subfield of two Galois fields is Galois and that a number fixed by a substitution group modulo all powers of a prime ideal lies in the fixed field.

triage.modern_statement: We can't tell exactly what the note asks. The best reading is that Hilbert wanted an integral representation for the Epstein-type zeta functions Z(s,ω) on this page, or for the sum of products Σ Z(s,ω)Z(1−s,ω). For Z(s,ω) alone, that means writing it as a Mellin transform of a theta series, roughly Γ(s)π^{-s}Z(s,ω) = ∫_0^∞ (θ_ω(t) − 1) t^{s−1} dt. That formula gives the analytic continuation and the functional equation s ↔ 1−s, and it leads to Kronecker's limit formula. I did not find a closed integral formula for the sum of products, and the two-word note doesn't say which object Hilbert meant.
triage.answered_by: If the note refers to a single Epstein zeta function, the theta-function integral representation was already standard by about 1903. It comes from Riemann's 1859 theta-function method, and Paul Epstein used it for general Epstein zeta functions in 'Zur Theorie allgemeiner Zetafunctionen', Math. Ann. 56 (1903), 615–644. I found nothing identifying who, if anyone, answered the question for the specific sum of products Hilbert was looking at.

evidence.claim: Paul Epstein's 1903 Math. Ann. paper extended the Riemann zeta function to series built from positive definite quadratic forms, which are now called Epstein zeta functions. He proved they continue meromorphically to the whole plane.
Bibliographic record: Epstein, Zur Theorie allgemeiner Zetafunctionen, Mathematische Annalen 56 (1903), 615–644.
The usual way to continue the Epstein zeta function analytically is through its integral representation in terms of Jacobi theta functions.
The meromorphic continuation and functional equation of Epstein zeta functions are proved by Poisson summation, following Riemann's proof for ζ(s). That work is linked to Kronecker limit formulas.
Kronecker's limit formula is the evaluation of ζ'_A(0) for the Epstein zeta function in terms of modular forms. The cited paper uses Mellin transform and Mellin inversion.

triage.why: The note is only the two words 'Integral Darstellung?' and gives no formula or object. If it means Z(s,ω), the answer has been standard since Riemann and Epstein (1903), and Epstein zeta functions and Kronecker limit formulas are still studied (see the 2022 arXiv paper above). If it means the sum Σ Z(s,ω)Z(1−s,ω), I found no specific source, so I can't say whether it was solved. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Without the page itself, it is too fragmentary to place confidently.
